plan.curriculum: English 2.0, Literacy and Language, Years 5 and 6: writing body paragraphs that open with a topic sentence, support it with evidence, and use linking words to guide the reader
plan.shape: mine, ours, yours again: put a jumbled zoo paragraph back together, watch it built, practise topic sentences and linking words, write one class paragraph together, then write two of their own
plan.criticalFeature: the first sentence of a body paragraph is the claim; every other sentence proves it or sells it
decisionPoints: the Find the topic sentence round
the choice check: the best topic sentence
the exit board: a topic sentence written for new proof
plan.anchor: Claim it. Prove it. Sell it. In a body paragraph: topic sentence, proof, This means...
plan.catchUp: Missed Session 1? Five minutes with the Session 1 Supported Worksheet (reader, position, two reasons), then write body paragraph 1 with the frame.

studentTools: Big piece plan and the introduction (writing books)
Writing books (draft on every second line)
routineIcons: Write it, chin it, show me
Point to A, B or C
boardSetup: The class shade letter introduction from Session 1
Paragraph recipe: Claim it (topic sentence), Prove it (fact or example), Sell it (This means...)
Linking words by job: first, next, strongest, example, result

resources.label: Worksheet
resources.description: Short warm-up on topic sentences and linking words, then plan both body paragraphs. The writing goes in writing books.
resources.title: Build Your Body

steps: Does it make a claim?
Could other sentences prove it?
Then it is a topic sentence.

items.prompt: Sort the sentences: TOPIC SENTENCE or PROOF.
cards: Tap water costs far less than bottled water.
Every classroom needs a water filter.
Last week the oval flooded twice.

Topic sentence: Every classroom needs a water filter.
Proof: Tap water costs far less than bottled water.
Last week the oval flooded twice.

steps: Read the job in brackets.
Pick a linking word for that job.
Add a comma after it.

items.prompt: Write a linking word for each job.
rows: ___, shade protects us from UV. (first reason)
The oval flooded. ___, sport was cancelled. (a result)
Pets calm us. ___, our class fish settles us after lunch. (an example)
answers: ___, shade protects us from UV. (first reason)
The oval flooded. ___, sport was cancelled. (a result)
Pets calm us. ___, our class fish settles us after lunch. (an example)

items.prompt: Sam squashed two reasons into one paragraph. Find the problem and fix it.
work: Firstly, dogs need exercise. Also the park has no fence, and cars are dangerous for dogs.
items.answer: Two reasons in one paragraph. Fix: start a new paragraph with its own topic sentence: Secondly, the park needs a fence to keep dogs safe.

steps: Claim it: linking word and topic sentence.
Prove it: a fact or an example.
Sell it: This means... why the reader should care.
example.answer: Firstly, bears need more space. Proof: some roam an area bigger than Tasmania. This means...

items.prompt: Plan both paragraphs in a few words. Then write them in your writing book, every second line.
answers: Firstly, + reason 1 from the plan as one sure sentence
a fact, number, example or expert, and who said it
This means... why it matters to this reader
Most importantly, + reason 2 as one sure sentence
a fact, number, example or expert, and who said it
This means... why it matters to this reader

resources.tip: Written both paragraphs? Grab the Extension.

resources.label: Extension
resources.description: Early finisher option: upgrade weak topic sentences, then sell the same proof to two different readers.
resources.title: Extension: Paragraph Power
resources.subtitle: Strong claims. Proof that sells.

steps: Ask: what am I arguing?
Say it as one sure claim.
Check a busy reader would get my point.
example.answer: Strong: Zoos cannot give polar bears the space they need.

items.prompt: Rewrite each weak topic sentence as a strong claim.
rows: Homework is a thing kids do.
answers: e.g. Every school should allow a reading dog in the library.
e.g. Our council must plant more street trees.
Homework is a thing kids do.
e.g. Primary students should not get homework on weekends.

example.prompt: Proof: bears roam huge distances. Reader: a Year 3 class.
steps: Read the claim and the proof.
Think about what this reader cares about.
Start with This means...
example.answer: This means a zoo bear can never go exploring, and that's not fair.

items.prompt: Claim: our school needs a vegetable garden. Proof: imagine our class survey found 18 of 25 kids would eat food they grew. Write a This means... sentence for the principal, then a different one for a Year 3 class.
items.answer: Principal: e.g. This means a garden could help more students eat healthy food at school. Year 3: e.g. This means you could eat carrots you grew yourself.

steps: Read the job.

So: Firstly,

slides.notes: Open the session: today the middle of the piece, two body paragraphs that prove the point.
Print the Worksheet for everyone, the Extension for early finishers and the Supported Worksheet for students who need it. Keep the class shade introduction from Session 1 on the board.

slides.learningIntention: We are learning to write body paragraphs that start with a clear topic sentence and prove it.
successCriteria: I can find the topic sentence of a paragraph.
I can write a body paragraph that claims it, proves it and sells it.
I can use linking words to guide my reader from one paragraph to the next.

beats: POINT to the learning intention.
SAY: Yesterday you told your reader what you want. Today you prove it.
SAY: Let's read the I can lines together.
Cue: Everyone, together, on three... one, two, three.
SAY: Finding the topic sentence is where everyone starts.
Writing two paragraphs that claim, prove and sell is today's big goal.
notes.prep: SC1 finding the topic sentence is reachable for all; SC2 the claim, prove, sell paragraph is the core; SC3 linking words is the stretch.

slides.title: Put it back together

notes.answer: B, C, A - claim it, prove it, sell it
beats: SAY: Here are three sentences from one paragraph of my zoo letter.
They've been jumbled up, so let's fix them.
ASK: Which sentence should start the paragraph?
10 sec. Cue: Voices off. Point... now. Hold your point.
EXPECT: pointing to B
ASK: What's the whole order, and why? Tell your partner.
20 sec. Cue: Partner A first. You have 20 seconds. Go.
Eyes back in 3, 2, 1.
EXPECT: B, C, A. Claim it, prove it, sell it.
SAY: That's our anchor again. B claims it, C proves it, and A sells it.
Every body paragraph you write today follows that order.
trap: starting with the fact because it's the most interesting.
Fix: ask what is this paragraph arguing? Student moves the claim first.
notes.prep: Mixed-start ordering task (megaprompt 19a); the order lives only in these notes. Re-grounds the anchor for anyone who missed a session. 3 minutes.

visual.text:
A: This means a zoo bear spends its whole life in a space smaller than one day's walk.
B: Firstly, polar bears need far more space than any zoo can give.
C: In the wild, some polar bears roam an area bigger than Tasmania.

slides.prompt: Which sentence should start the paragraph?

slides.meaning: The first sentence of a paragraph. It tells the reader what the paragraph will prove.
slides.example: Most importantly, polar bears are built for the cold.

notes.answer: the first sentence, the one that says what the paragraph proves
beats: POINT to the words. SAY: These words are topic sentence. Say them with me.
Cue: Everyone, together, on three... one, two, three.
SAY: Busy readers often read only the first sentence of each paragraph.
So the topic sentence has to carry your claim, like a flag.
ASK: Does the example make a claim or give a fact?
5 sec. Cue: Fingers at your chest, voices off... show me. 1 claim, 2 fact.
EXPECT: 1, a claim
trap: a topic sentence that just names the topic, like Zoos.
Fix: student adds what they think about it.
notes.prep: The flag picture is the Claim it picture used all term.

slides.title: Mine: watch me build a body paragraph
slides.extract: Firstly, polar bears need far more space than any zoo can give. In the wild, some polar bears roam an area bigger than Tasmania. Even a large zoo enclosure is a tiny fraction of that. This means a zoo bear spends its whole life in a space smaller than one day's walk. No animal built to wander should live behind a wall.
highlights: Firstly, polar bears need far more space
slides.source: Model letter, written for this session

notes.answer: 1 finger - the first sentence carries the claim
beats: POINT to Firstly.
SAY: Claim it. Prove it. Sell it. Firstly tells my reader this is reason one,
and my claim comes straight from my plan.
POINT to Tasmania.
SAY: Now I prove it. A fact the director can check is hard to argue with.
POINT to This means.
SAY: Then I sell it. This means tells the director why the fact matters.
ASK: A busy reader only reads one sentence. Which number should it be?
5 sec. Cue: Fingers at your chest, voices off... show me.
EXPECT: 1 finger
trap: proof with no This means, so the fact just sits there.
Fix: student adds This means and one reason it matters.
notes.stretch: Write a different last line that sells it to a Year 3 class.
notes.help: Supported Worksheet: a starter for each part.
notes.prep: Mine: the zoo letter's first body paragraph. Critical feature: the first sentence is the claim; the rest prove or sell it.

slides.title: Linking words do a job

beats: POINT to the Job column.
SAY: Linking words are signposts. Each one tells the reader what's coming next.
SAY: My second paragraph is my strongest reason, the cold.
So I need a word that says this matters most.
ASK: Which linking word should start my second paragraph?
15 sec. Cue: Write it... Chin it... Show me.
EXPECT: Most importantly, or Above all,
trap: using And or Also to start every paragraph.
Fix: student finds the job in the table and swaps the word.
notes.stretch: Which linking word could join two sentences inside a paragraph?
notes.help: Copy the table into the back of your writing book to use while you write.
notes.prep: The table goes on the board and stays up during the writing.

slides.prompt: Start each body paragraph with the word that does the job.

slides.title: Find the topic sentence
slides.pivot: ask which sentence the others are proving
slides.followUp: cold call one student: how do the other two help it?

items.answer: B - the claim; A and C prove it
items.extract:
A: It also keeps us calm.
B: A class pet teaches responsibility.
C: Feeding it is a shared job.

items.answer: A - the claim; B and C prove it
items.extract:
A: Plastic straws should be banned.
B: They last hundreds of years.
C: Paper ones work just as well.

items.answer: C - the claim; A and B prove it
items.extract:
A: Our basketball court floods every winter.
B: Kids slip and get hurt.
C: The court needs better drains.

say: Each set is one paragraph, but the sentences are mixed up.
Find the one that should go first, the claim.
trap: pointing to the first sentence on the screen.
Fix: ask which one do the others prove? Student points again.
notes.stretch: Say the whole paragraph in claim, prove, sell order.
notes.help: Look for should or needs, because they often mark the claim.
notes.prep: Guided practice, mixed positions so the first line is not always the answer. SC1.

slides.ask: Which sentence should go first, the one the other two prove?

slides.title: Which is the best topic sentence?
slides.prompt: A paragraph arguing that school should start later.

options.misconception: picks a sentence on the topic that claims nothing

options.text: Most kids fall asleep after ten.
options.misconception: picks a piece of proof instead of the claim

options.text: A later start would help kids learn more.

notes.answer: C - it makes the claim the paragraph will prove
beats: SAY: Only one of these could lead the paragraph. Think about what it's arguing.
ASK: Which is the best topic sentence?
15 sec. Cue: Voices off. Point... now. Hold your point.
EXPECT: pointing to C
SCAN the room, back row first.
80%+ -> reveal, then cold call a B: where could B go instead?
Less -> test each with should or would, re-ask.
REVEAL after pointing is scanned.
SAY: It's C, because it makes a claim. B is great proof for the next sentence.
trap: choosing B because it has a fact in it.
Fix: ask does it say what should happen? Student re-chooses.
notes.prep: Decision point before drafting: can they tell a claim from proof?

slides.title: Link it
slides.pivot: read the job in brackets, then find it in the table
slides.followUp: cold call one board: which job told you?

items.text: ___, a pool would teach kids to swim safely. (my strongest reason)
items.say: It's Most importantly, or Above all. Tick it or fix it.

items.text: The canteen sells only lollies at recess. ___, kids are starving by lunch. (a result)
items.say: It's As a result. Tick it or fix it.

items.text: ___, a garden would cut our food waste. (my second reason)
items.say: It's Secondly, or In addition. Tick it or fix it.

say: Read the job in brackets, then write the linking word that does it.
trap: writing For example before a new reason.
Fix: student reads the job again and checks the table.
notes.stretch: Write a second word that does the same job.
notes.help: Use the linking words table on the board.
notes.prep: Guided practice on SC3, mixed jobs. SC3.

slides.ask: Which linking word does the job in the brackets?

slides.title: Ours: let's build our body paragraphs

rows: Firstly, shade keeps us safe from the sun.
SunSmart says we need sun protection from August to April.

slides.prompt: You write the Sell it line. I scribe the paragraph.

notes.answer: e.g. This means we could play outside all year without burning.
beats: SAY: Now we build ours. The claim and proof are done.
You do the selling.
ASK: Write our This means sentence. Why should the principal care?
45 sec. Cue: Write it... Chin it... Show me.
EXPECT: we can play outside safely all year
SCAN boards for a reason the principal would care about.
80%+ -> cold call two boards, class picks one.
Less -> start it together: This means we can..., re-ask.
ASK: Which linking word starts body 2, our strongest reason?
10 sec. Cue: Write it... Chin it... Show me.
EXPECT: Most importantly,
SCRIBE body 2: Most importantly, shade keeps equipment cool. Our slide burns.
trap: a This means line that repeats the proof.
Fix: ask so what? Student adds why.
notes.prep: Ours: scribe body 1 together, then body 2 from the plan, so the class letter has both. Keep it for Session 3. SOURCES: SunSmart Victoria, sun protection mid-August to end of April.

slides.title: Yours: write your two body paragraphs
slides.task: Do the warm-up, plan both paragraphs, then write them in your writing book, every second line.
slides.visualLabel: Claim it. Prove it. Sell it.
slides.extendedTask: a short warm-up, the two-paragraph plan, then both body paragraphs drafted in writing books

notes.answer: two body paragraphs, each with a topic sentence, proof and This means
beats: POINT to the task.
SAY: The warm-up takes three minutes.
Then plan both paragraphs and get writing.
SAY: Let's read the steps together.
Cue: Everyone, together, on three... one, two, three.
CONFERENCE first with anyone from yesterday's exit list.
ASK: Swap books. Read only the topic sentences. Can you say their argument?
20 sec. Cue: Partner A first. You have 20 seconds. Go.
Eyes back in 3, 2, 1.
EXPECT: You think we should...
TIME 25 minutes: warm-up 3, plan 5, writing 17, partner swap at 22.
trap: two reasons squashed into one paragraph.
Fix: student splits it and gives the second its own topic sentence.
notes.stretch: upgrade weak topic sentences, then sell one proof to two readers.
notes.help: Supported Worksheet: claim or proof, the linking word, a three-starter frame.
notes.prep: Yours: body 1 and body 2 of the big piece. Every second line, ready for Week 5. SC2 and SC3.

slides.title: Show what you know
questions: Walking gets your heart pumping before class. It's free, and you can chat with friends on the way.
Write the topic sentence that should start this paragraph.

notes.answer: e.g. Kids should walk to school whenever they can.
beats: SAY: Here's a paragraph with its first sentence missing. Write the claim it proves.
ASK: Write the topic sentence that should start this paragraph.
45 sec. Cue: Write it... Chin it... Show me.
EXPECT: one sure claim about walking to school
RECORD who writes another fact, or just Walking. They're tomorrow's first conference.
trap: writing another reason instead of the claim.
Fix: none now, record the name.
notes.prep: Exit evidence for SC2 on a new paragraph. One board per student.

slides.reflectionPrompt: Read only your two topic sentences to your partner. Can they guess your whole argument?

notes.answer: open - the partner can say the argument from the topic sentences
beats: SAY: Let's read our I can lines together.
Cue: Everyone, together, on three... one, two, three.
ASK: How sure are you that both paragraphs claim it, prove it and sell it?
5 sec. Cue: Thumbs only, voices off. Show me... now.
EXPECT: thumbs up, sideways or down
RECORD each thumb down beside the exit boards.
A thumb up with a wrong exit board matters most.
ASK: Read only your topic sentences. Can your partner guess your argument?
30 sec. Cue: Partner B reads first. You have 30 seconds. Go.
Eyes back in 3, 2, 1.
EXPECT: You're arguing that...
notes.prep: Self-assessment read beside the exit boards. SC2.
